new_statements.quote: El acento y el alargamiento (ya descrito arriba) son los dos únicos fonemas suprasegmentales. El acento parece predecible en la primera sílaba de la raíz, aún cuando ésta vaya acompañada de algunos prefijos y sufijos que no llevan acento: (1) góges 'perro', wíhig-em 'fino', excepto en los siguientes casos: a. El sufijo locativo -Cam lleva el acento de la palabra: (2) téesem 'fogón', tesem-tám 'en el fogón'. b. En las palabras formadas por dos raíces, la raíz modificada lleva el acento: 'uus-gát 'arco'. c. Las partículas de forma monosilábica no llevan acento ... d. Los préstamos del español y de otros idiomas llevan el acento en la sílaba final ... e. Las raíces nominales y verbales que presentan reduplicación parcial, cambian el acento a la parte reduplicada: kély 'hombre', ké-kely 'hombres'.
new_statements.translation: Stress and lengthening (already described above) are the only two suprasegmental phonemes. Stress appears to be predictable on the first syllable of the root, even when the root is accompanied by prefixes and suffixes, which do not bear stress: góges 'dog', wíhig-em 'fine'; except in the following cases: a. the locative suffix -Cam takes the word stress: téesem 'hearth', tesem-tám 'at the hearth'; b. in words formed from two roots, the modified (head) root bears the stress: 'uus-gát 'bow'; c. monosyllabic particles bear no stress; d. loans from Spanish and other languages are stressed on the final syllable; e. nominal and verbal roots with partial reduplication shift the stress to the reduplicated part: kély 'man', ké-kely 'men'.
new_statements.citation: Escalante H., Roberto & Zarina Estrada Fernández. 1993. Textos y gramática del pima bajo. Hermosillo: Universidad de Sonora (Departamento de Letras y Lingüística).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (root-initial); affixes are unstressed, so in unprefixed words stress is word-initial. A CV- reduplicative prefix takes the stress (i.e. stress stays leftmost in the reduplicated stem); the locative suffix -Cam (-tám etc.) attracts word stress; in root+root compounds the second (head/modified) root is stressed; monosyllabic particles are unstressed; loanwords keep final (or original Spanish) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Locative suffix -Cam is stressed (tesem-tám); compounds stress the modified root ('uus-gát); monosyllabic particles unstressed (chich, wen); Spanish/Ópata loans final-stressed (karmiyól, garbáns, ariwéch), footnote 15: or retaining original Spanish stress (beséer, asúkul, palatísam); partial reduplication moves stress onto the reduplicant (ké-kely, mú-m(u)k-im); fn. 14 long vowels shorten in compounds/plurals/postpositional phrases; fn. 16 post-tonic vowel tends to drop after reduplication. Author hedges with 'parece predecible'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement over root+affixes (citation forms from elicited vocabulary); describes the Maycoba (Yécora municipality, Sonora) dialect from Escalante's 1961-62 fieldwork. Estrada Fernández 1998 (Yepachi, Chihuahua) gives no rule but its accent-marked syllabification examples (pá.risa, báa.mag vs ko.nóo.li, ma.kúu.si, la.lóob) show second-syllable accent when that syllable has a long vowel, hinting at a weight-sensitive initial/second pattern in that dialect that the 1993 rule does not discuss.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule is Escalante's grammar sketch of the Maycoba dialect (municipio de Yécora, Sonora; 'eastern' Pima Bajo), fieldwork 1961-62, published 1993 with Estrada Fernández. Estrada Fernández 1998 (ALIM 21) describes the Yepachi, Chihuahua dialect and gives only accent-marked examples, no rule. Both fall under pima1248 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes used here). Névome (Smith 1862) is the 17th-c. colonial stage of the same language.

sources.note: Cap. 2 Fonología, §2.4 Acento (pp. 37-38): stress and vowel length are the only suprasegmental phonemes; stress 'parece predecible en la primera sílaba de la raíz', prefixes/suffixes unstressed; exceptions: locative -Cam takes the word stress (tesem-tám), in two-root compounds the modified root is stressed ('uus-gát), monosyllabic particles unstressed, Spanish/other loans stressed on final syllable (fn: or keep original Spanish stress), partial CV- reduplication shifts stress to the reduplicant (ké-kely). Grammar sketch by Escalante on the Maycoba (Sonora) dialect, fieldwork 1961-62.
